item.title: Estate agents escape blame as almost three-quarters of home movers face delays
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent research reveals that 72% of UK home movers faced delays during their property transactions, yet estate agents largely escaped blame for these hold-ups. The average home move now takes 216 days from listing to completion – 36 days longer than in 2019 according to Rightmove data. While the property industry acknowledges these challenges, professionals remain divided on potential solutions.

Where delays occur – and who bears the blame

The home-moving process has become notably slower, with sellers typically waiting 62 days to secure a buyer before facing a further 154-day journey to completion. When delayed movers identified responsibility, half pointed to conveyancers or solicitors, while 40% attributed delays to the other party in the transaction. Only 5% held estate agents accountable.

Regional variations paint a striking picture, with Londoners (80%), East Midlands residents (79%), and movers in Wales and the North West (78%) reporting the highest delay rates. Scotland fared considerably better at 43%, suggesting different market dynamics or legal processes may influence transaction speeds.

Industry divided on solutions

Property professionals show little consensus on how to streamline transactions. Estate agents predominantly advocate for:

  • Faster communication (33%)
  • Shared case tracking (25%)
  • Integrated digital systems (10%)

Conveyancers take a different view, prioritising:

  • Better understanding between professions (23%)
  • Clearer client expectations (21%)
  • Only 13% see faster communication as the primary solution

Mortgage brokers balanced their preferences equally between improved communication and agreed service standards (22% each), while nearly 30% of surveyors doubted any proposed measures would significantly enhance working relationships.

Professional relationships under scrutiny

The research uncovered notable disparities in how property professionals perceive their working relationships. Estate agents appear more positive about their collaborations, with 67% describing relationships with conveyancers as good – a sentiment only reciprocated by 50% of conveyancers. Similar gaps exist between agents and surveyors (54% versus 44%) and in mortgage advice relationships (58% of agents versus 54% of brokers holding positive views).

These findings suggest that while the industry recognises transaction delays as problematic, solutions may require more coordinated efforts between different professional groups. Homeowners embarking on a move might benefit from understanding these potential friction points when planning their property journey.

item.title: Estate agents face September slowdown as viewings take a hit
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The start of the autumn property market could see a slowdown, with many parents of school-aged children expecting their house-hunting activities to take a backseat as family routines resume. According to recent research by House Buyer Bureau, nearly nine in ten (88%) parents anticipate booking or attending fewer property viewings during the first few weeks of the new school term. This trend could have a ripple effect on the broader property market, as buyers juggle childcare and other commitments.

Family Commitments Impact Property Searches

For parents, the return to school often means a shift in priorities. The study found that 86% of respondents expect to spend less time actively searching for a new home, with childcare responsibilities cited as the biggest obstacle by 24% of parents. Other challenges include school drop-offs and pick-ups (22%), after-school clubs and activities (13%), and the general demands of returning to work and re-establishing family routines (11%). As a result, estate agents may need to adapt their strategies to accommodate these changing schedules. For instance, 37% of parents prefer viewings during school hours, while 35% favour weekends. Evenings are the preferred time for 20%, with just 8% opting for after-school appointments.

Increased Reliance on Digital Tools

With buyers having less time for in-person viewings, digital marketing tools are likely to play a more prominent role in the property market. Nearly four in five (79%) parents expect to rely more heavily on online listings, virtual tours, or video viewings when searching for their next home. This shift towards digital solutions could help estate agents maintain engagement with buyers during this period of reduced activity.

However, the slowdown may not be limited to viewings alone. The research also highlights potential delays in sales progression, with 92% of respondents stating that school commitments could slow their purchase process. Tasks such as dealing with paperwork, attending mortgage appointments, and managing surveys may prove more challenging amidst busy family schedules. Three-quarters of parents believe it could take more than a month before they can fully focus on their property search again, with just 12% expecting to return to normal activity within a week.

Longer-Term Effects on the Market

Chris Hodgkinson, managing director of House Buyer Bureau, noted that the impact of school commitments on the property market may extend beyond the initial weeks of September. He explained, “Traditionally, September marks the point at which the property market starts to regain momentum after the summer holidays. However, for parents, the return to school can leave little time for searching for a home, attending viewings, or progressing a purchase. This may not be a short-lived blip, as many parents believe it could take over a month before they can fully re-engage with the market.”

Estate agents and sellers may need to exercise patience during this period, as buyers navigate the demands of the school year. Flexibility in scheduling and a greater emphasis on digital tools could help bridge the gap, ensuring that interest in properties remains steady even as physical viewings decline.

item.title: Renters’ Rights Act piles more work on letting agents
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The Renters’ Rights Act, introduced on 1 May, has significantly impacted the workload of letting agents across the UK. According to recent research by Propoly, 73% of property professionals report an increase in administrative tasks since the legislation came into force. For a quarter of respondents, the effect on their business has been particularly pronounced, with compliance and record-keeping emerging as the primary sources of additional work.

Increased Administrative Demands

One of the key challenges identified by letting agents is the heightened administrative burden. Compliance and record-keeping were cited by 18% of respondents as the most time-consuming tasks, followed by rent reviews (16%) and managing possessions and tenancy endings (14%). The Act has also necessitated closer collaboration between lettings and property management teams, with half of respondents noting that staff now need to work more cohesively.

Technology, while often seen as a solution to streamline processes, appears to be adding to the complexity for some agents. Only 17% of businesses use a single, integrated system to manage the additional work created by the Renters’ Rights Act. Two-thirds rely on multiple disconnected systems, and another 17% depend heavily on emails, spreadsheets, and other manual processes. This fragmentation can lead to inefficiencies, with 61% of respondents reporting that staff often have to transfer, re-enter, or duplicate information across different platforms.

The Need for Better Integration

The lack of integration between systems is a significant issue for many letting agents. More than half (52%) believe that better links between their systems would improve efficiency. Landlord communication and decision-making were identified as areas that could benefit most from improved integration, followed by tenant referencing, compliance, and tenant communications.

Sim Sekhon, group chief executive officer at Propoly, commented: “Over 100 days since the introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act, it’s clear that the impact extends beyond just additional work. Lettings businesses now need to rethink how they organise their people, processes, and technology to ensure information flows efficiently between teams and systems involved in managing a tenancy.”

Ongoing Compliance Challenges

Compliance remains a major concern for letting agents, with 28% of respondents expecting it to become their biggest operational challenge under the Renters’ Rights Act. Maintaining profitability whilst managing the additional workload was flagged by 21% of respondents, while 16% pointed to the overall administrative burden as a key issue.

As the sector continues to adapt to these changes, the focus will likely remain on finding ways to streamline processes and improve efficiency. For many agents, investing in better technology and fostering closer collaboration between teams could be essential steps in navigating the challenges posed by the Renters’ Rights Act.

With the legislation still in its early stages, it remains to be seen how letting agents will continue to evolve their practices to meet these new demands. However, one thing is clear: the Renters’ Rights Act has ushered in a period of significant change for the industry.

item.title: Renters’ Rights Act drives landlords towards greater use of guarantors
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Landlords are increasingly turning to guarantor requests for tenants following recent changes under the Renters’ Rights Act, according to new research. With the legislation now preventing landlords from asking for more than one month’s rent upfront, many are tightening their income checks and seeking alternative safeguards – potentially creating challenges for renters without access to guarantors.

Guarantor requests on the rise

The Summer 2026 Lettings Report surveyed over 1,500 landlords and tenants across England and Wales, revealing that 54% of landlords now more frequently request guarantors when prospective tenants fail standard affordability checks. This shift comes as the Renters’ Rights Act removes the option for landlords to request multiple months’ rent in advance as security.

Among tenants without personal guarantors, the research found:

  • 51% would seek cheaper accommodation
  • 16% would pause their property search entirely
  • Only 18% would consider paid guarantor services

Awareness of commercial guarantor services remains strikingly low, with 74% of tenants completely unfamiliar with the concept and just 2% having ever used such services. Separate research indicates 34% of renters didn’t understand what a guarantor was when first asked to provide one.

Alternative protections gaining traction

Whilst 28% of landlords reported no change in their guarantor policies and 13% maintained existing practices, some are exploring different risk-management solutions. Rent guarantee insurance appears to be growing in popularity, with 37% of landlords already holding policies and a further 19% considering coverage. However, 17% remained unaware such products existed.

The English Housing Survey 2024-25 found that 20% of private renters already required guarantors before the legislative changes, suggesting the practice was already widespread in certain market segments. Industry experts suggest that clearer communication about tenant verification options may benefit both landlords and renters navigating the new regulatory environment.

Allison Thompson of LRG noted: “Landlords need confidence in a tenancy’s affordability, particularly now that advance rent payments are no longer available as an additional safeguard.” The findings highlight how regulatory changes can unintentionally reshape rental market dynamics, with implications for housing accessibility.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Two leading UK property consultancies have announced high-profile appointments this month, signalling continued confidence in the specialist rural and commercial property sectors. Knight Frank has named a new head for its national country department, while BTG Eddisons has expanded its North West team with an experienced commercial property director.

Knight Frank appoints new country property head

Will Matthews, known professionally as "Stan", has taken over as head of Knight Frank's national country department following Edward Rook's decade-long tenure. The London-based team handles premium country properties, averaging over £400m in annual sales during Rook's leadership.

Matthews brings two decades of experience at Knight Frank to the role, having joined in 2003. He initially specialised in prime country house sales before moving into farms and estates. Since 2022, he has led the firm's Farms and Estates team while advising on rural property transactions nationwide.

Rook commented: "Will understands every aspect of the country market. The department will continue to thrive under his leadership." Despite current market challenges, the team completed £173m of prime country house sales in early 2026.

Matthews noted the enduring demand for specialist rural property advice, stating: "Our clients continue to seek expertise across country houses, farms and estates. We look forward to building on our success."

Commercial property veteran joins BTG Eddisons

Meanwhile, commercial property consultancy BTG Eddisons has strengthened its North West operations with the appointment of Ian Steele as director. Steele joins after seven years as principal at Avison Young's Liverpool office, bringing over 30 years' experience in the North West commercial property market.

Steele will focus on office agency and development markets across Liverpool and Manchester, working alongside directors Robert Diggle and David Baker. His appointment reflects growing demand for commercial property expertise in the region.

Luke Tillison, BTG Eddisons' head of transactional, said: "Ian is well established in the Liverpool market with an exceptional network. His expertise will prove invaluable as we expand our regional services."

These strategic appointments suggest both firms remain optimistic about long-term prospects in their respective property sectors, despite current economic uncertainties. Homeowners and investors may wish to monitor how these leadership changes affect market dynamics in coming months.

item.title: 7 in 10 investors plan BTR investment
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research reveals growing enthusiasm for build-to-rent (BTR) properties among UK property investors, with approximately 70% reportedly considering adding these residential assets to their portfolios. This emerging trend reflects shifting investment strategies as the rental market continues to evolve.

Build-to-rent sector gains momentum

The BTR market has seen significant growth in recent years, attracting both institutional investors and private landlords. Industry analysts suggest this surge in interest stems from several factors, including consistent tenant demand, professional management structures, and the potential for stable long-term yields. Many investors appear to be diversifying their holdings beyond traditional buy-to-let properties to capitalise on these benefits.

Modern BTR developments often feature purpose-designed rental accommodation with premium amenities, appealing particularly to young professionals and families seeking flexible living arrangements. These properties typically come with professional management services, reducing the hands-on responsibilities that often accompany standard rental investments.

Changing investment landscape

The property investment landscape continues to shift, with many investors reassessing their strategies in response to regulatory changes and market conditions. The research suggests that investors are increasingly looking at BTR schemes as a way to future-proof their portfolios whilst potentially benefiting from economies of scale.

Several factors appear to be driving this trend:

  • Strong and sustained demand for quality rental accommodation in key UK cities
  • Potential for institutional-grade management and maintenance standards
  • Attractive yields compared to some traditional buy-to-let investments
  • Growing tenant preference for professionally managed rental properties

Property professionals note that whilst BTR requires different considerations compared to traditional buy-to-let, the sector offers distinct advantages for investors seeking to expand or diversify their residential property holdings. The hands-off nature of many BTR investments could prove particularly appealing to those looking to reduce day-to-day management responsibilities.

As the UK rental market continues to evolve, build-to-rent properties are emerging as an increasingly important component of many investors' strategies. Those considering this approach may wish to seek professional financial advice to understand how BTR investments might fit within their overall portfolio and long-term objectives.

item.title: UKCertifID trust mark to transform homebuying
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A new digital verification scheme promising to simplify the property purchasing process has been launched in the UK. The UKCertifID trust mark aims to create a standardised approach to identity checks across all parties involved in home buying transactions.

How the trust mark could improve the buying process

The property sector currently requires multiple identity verifications when buyers interact with different professionals. Estate agents, mortgage brokers, lenders and conveyancers each conduct separate checks, creating duplication that slows down transactions.

The new scheme could potentially:

  • Reduce repetitive identity verification requests
  • Speed up the overall conveyancing timeline
  • Lower fraud risks through standardised security checks
  • Create a smoother experience for home movers

Industry-wide adoption challenges

While the concept shows promise, widespread implementation across the fragmented property sector may prove challenging. Many stakeholders operate different systems and processes. Homebuyers might not see immediate benefits until critical mass adoption occurs among:

  • High street estate agency chains
  • Major mortgage lenders
  • National conveyancing firms

The scheme's success could hinge on whether industry participants recognise the long-term efficiency gains outweigh short-term integration costs.

For homeowners considering a property purchase, it may be worth enquiring whether professionals involved in their transaction support the UKCertifID trust mark. As digital transformation continues across the sector, such initiatives could gradually reduce some traditional pain points in the home moving process.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent developments in the UK property sector have seen notable appointments and promotions, highlighting the industry’s focus on leadership and operational excellence. From global finance roles to local lettings and sales progression, these changes reflect the dynamic nature of the property market.

Knight Frank Welcomes New Group CFO

Knight Frank, a leading global property consultancy, has announced the appointment of Chris Davis as its new Group Chief Financial Officer (CFO). Davis, who previously held the role on an interim basis, has now been confirmed as the permanent CFO following a competitive selection process. He will also join the firm’s Group Executive Board, taking charge of Knight Frank’s global finance function.

With over 24 years of international business experience, Davis brings a wealth of expertise to the role. His career includes CFO positions at Marlet Property Group and G.Network, as well as board-level roles at Hilding Anders. He also spent a decade as an equity partner at AlixPartners and THM Partners. Davis will oversee financial performance and support the delivery of Knight Frank’s international strategy.

Davis commented on his appointment, stating, “This is an exciting time to step into the role of Group CFO at Knight Frank. The position requires a sophisticated understanding of data-led decision-making and commercial forecasting, and I am looking forward to contributing to the firm’s growth.”

William Beardmore-Gray, Senior Partner and Group Chair at Knight Frank, added, “Chris has already shown excellent leadership and a deep understanding of our business. His extensive CFO experience makes him the ideal candidate to guide Knight Frank into its next phase of growth.”

Cavendish Announces Internal Promotions

Meanwhile, Cavendish, a Chester-based property agency, has promoted three of its staff members at its Grosvenor Street office. These promotions span roles in sales progression and lettings, reflecting the agency’s commitment to nurturing talent and enhancing its services.

Emily Pickering has been promoted from Sales Progressor to Senior Sales Progressor. item.title: UK’s best property auction houses revealed in new ranking
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New research has shed light on how UK property auction houses compare when it comes to success rates, buyer costs and investor suitability. The UK Auction House Performance Index, compiled by investment research specialists UncommonDeal, evaluates 12 prominent auction operators to help property buyers navigate this competitive market.

How auction houses compare

The index moves beyond simple sales volumes to assess auction providers across multiple investor-focused criteria. Findings reveal notable differences between operators, with top performers achieving consistently high scores across several key measures. Leading the rankings was Allsop with an overall performance score of 94/100, followed closely by Savills Auctions (91/100) and SDL Property Auctions (88/100).

The research suggests that successful auction houses tend to excel in areas such as:

  • High completion rates for properties listed
  • Transparent fee structures for buyers
  • Diverse property types across different price points
  • Strong geographic coverage across regions

What the rankings mean for buyers

While the index provides a useful comparative snapshot, prospective buyers might consider it as just one part of their research process. The rankings don't highlight individual lots or specific local market conditions, which can significantly influence investment outcomes.

Property investors may wish to examine several factors when choosing an auction house, including:

  • Historical success rates for similar properties
  • The clarity of legal packs and documentation
  • Additional buyer premiums and administrative fees
  • The auctioneer's specialism in certain property types

The index employs a weighted scoring system across six core categories relevant to property professionals, providing a standardised way to compare operators. Rather than declaring a single "best" auction house, it offers consistent benchmarks that reflect different strengths across the sector.

For those considering property auctions, these insights could help inform initial research while reinforcing the importance of thorough due diligence on individual lots and local market conditions before bidding.

item.title: Could Britain’s train stations unlock 1.2m new homes?
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Britain's major cities could potentially unlock space for over 1.2 million additional homes by increasing housing density around inner-city railway stations, according to new research from the Centre for Cities. The think tank's analysis suggests UK urban areas lag behind comparable cities in France and Japan when it comes to maximising development opportunities near transport hubs.

Untapped potential near transport hubs

The research highlights a striking disparity in housing density patterns between UK cities and their international counterparts. Unlike many G7 cities where density naturally increases around railway stations, British urban areas often show the opposite trend. Sheffield and Liverpool, for example, actually have lower housing densities near stations than in surrounding areas.

London represents the most significant opportunity, with capacity for an estimated 500,000 additional homes near stations. Other major cities show substantial potential too - Glasgow could accommodate around 183,000 more properties, while Manchester has space for approximately 134,000. These figures emerge from comparing current UK development patterns with those in similar French and Japanese cities.

The international development gap

Between 2011 and 2021, Britain's major cities built less than half the number of homes around train and tram stations achieved by comparable cities abroad. Manchester performed best outside London, delivering about 30,000 homes around inner-city stations during this period, including developments near Metrolink stops. The capital itself added roughly 300,000 station-adjacent homes.

While cities like Glasgow, Birmingham and Liverpool have increased development, they continue to underperform international peers. Researchers attribute this partly to smaller transport networks and lower housing delivery per station. Leeds and Bristol face additional constraints due to transport infrastructure that provides fewer suitable development sites near stations.

Addressing the housing shortage

The Centre for Cities estimates that closing this density gap around urban stations could reduce Britain's housing shortage by approximately 25%. Focusing development on areas with existing transport infrastructure offers several potential advantages:

  • Reduced need for costly new transport investments
  • Better access to employment centres for residents
  • More sustainable urban growth patterns
  • Revitalisation of underutilised urban spaces

As the housing crisis continues, policymakers and developers may wish to examine these findings closely. The research suggests that thoughtful densification around transport hubs could provide a practical solution to boost housing supply while making efficient use of existing infrastructure.

item.title: Mortgage approvals slump to lowest level in more than two years
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Mortgage approvals for home purchases in the UK have dropped to their lowest level in over two years, according to the latest data from the Bank of England. Figures reveal that just 56,053 mortgages were approved for house purchases in July, marking the lowest total since January 2024. This decline highlights the ongoing challenges facing the housing market, with higher borrowing costs and economic uncertainty continuing to dampen buyer activity.

What’s Behind the Decline?

The sharp fall in mortgage approvals reflects a broader slowdown in the housing market. July’s figures were down from 58,215 in June and remained below the six-month monthly average of approximately 60,800. Experts suggest that rising mortgage rates and wider economic pressures are deterring potential buyers. Lucian Cook, head of residential research at Savills, noted that affordability remains a key issue, with house prices gently declining when adjusted for inflation. However, higher mortgage costs have hindered any meaningful improvement in market activity.

Recent geopolitical tensions and elevated energy prices have also contributed to the subdued market. Hina Bhudia, partner at Knight Frank Finance, explained that these factors pushed mortgage rates higher during the summer, further impacting demand. While leading fixed rates have stabilised recently, with two-year fixed rates available as low as 4.45%, a sustained recovery may require rates to fall closer to 4%. Bhudia added that renewed hostilities in the Middle East and speculation ahead of the Budget could present additional risks to the market.

Remortgaging Activity Bucks the Trend

Whilst mortgage approvals for home purchases have declined, remortgaging activity has moved in the opposite direction. The Bank of England reported that approvals for borrowers switching to a different lender increased to around 34,500 in July, up from 34,100 in June. This suggests that homeowners may be seeking to secure better deals amidst rising interest rates, particularly as fixed-rate mortgage deals come to an end.

The Nationwide House Price Index also provided insight into the state of the housing market, showing little movement in property values. Average UK house prices increased by 0.2% month-on-month in August, following a slight decline of 0.1% in July. The average property was valued at £275,465, with annual house price growth standing at 1.6%. Whilst these figures indicate stability, they also reflect the cautious sentiment among buyers and sellers.

What Lies Ahead for the Housing Market?

Looking ahead, experts predict that the housing market is unlikely to see a significant turnaround in the near future. Cook emphasised that with inflation still working its way through the economy, sustained improvement in activity appears unlikely for the remainder of the year. Borrowers and homeowners may wish to carefully assess their options, particularly those nearing the end of fixed-rate deals, as remortgaging could offer a way to mitigate rising costs.

For now, the housing market remains in a period of adjustment, with affordability challenges and economic uncertainty shaping buyer behaviour. Whilst mortgage approvals have slumped, remortgaging activity highlights the importance of staying proactive in managing mortgage commitments.

item.title: HM Land Registry turns to AI in contact centre overhaul
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

HM Land Registry (HMLR) has announced a significant upgrade to its contact centre operations, with the introduction of a new AI-powered platform. The initiative, delivered by Route 101, aims to modernise customer support services and improve efficiency across its operations. The cloud-based system will replace the existing on-premises infrastructure and serve approximately 660 users across five sites.

What Does the New System Include?

The new platform will integrate voice and digital communication channels, supported by AI-assisted customer service tools. It will also feature analytics and workforce management technology from providers such as NiCE, Cognigy, and Calabrio. Designed to streamline operations, the system will enable HMLR to handle call volumes more effectively and provide real-time information to advisers when responding to enquiries.

One of the key benefits of the platform is its ability to support hybrid working arrangements. With AI-powered automation, the system will enhance efficiency across both voice and digital channels. It will also integrate seamlessly with HMLR’s current systems and services, ensuring a smooth transition. Additionally, the technology will be hosted in the UK, with robust security measures including role-based access controls, monitoring, and encrypted data protection.

Why Is This Upgrade Important?

HMLR plays a crucial role in maintaining the land and property register for England and Wales, covering over 90% of the land area and more than 27 million titles. Its contact centre handles enquiries from property professionals and the general public, making efficient customer support essential. The new system is expected to improve service delivery, reduce wait times, and provide advisers with the tools they need to resolve queries more effectively.

The upgrade also reflects HMLR’s commitment to embracing technological advancements. By leveraging AI and cloud-based solutions, the organisation aims to future-proof its operations and adapt to changing demands. Route 101, which secured the contract following a public sector procurement process, will oversee the design, integration, and ongoing support of the platform.

This move could have broader implications for the property sector, particularly for estate agents and conveyancers who rely on HMLR’s services. Enhanced efficiency and accessibility may lead to quicker turnaround times for property transactions, benefiting both professionals and homeowners.

As HMLR continues its digital transformation, this upgrade marks a significant step forward in improving customer experience and operational efficiency. With AI at its core, the new contact centre platform is poised to set a new standard for public sector service delivery.

item.title: Buy-to-let costs soar twice as fast as rental income
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Buy-to-let landlords are facing mounting financial pressures as rising costs outpace rental income growth, according to recent analysis of HMRC data. Lettings platform Hello Neighbour found that expenses now consume nearly 60p of every £1 earned in rent, up from 47.8% just five years ago. This trend highlights the growing challenges for property investors in the private rental sector.

Rising Costs Outstrip Rental Income

Over the past five years, buy-to-let expenses have surged by 56%, while rental income has increased by just 26%. In the 2024-25 financial year, landlords declared £34.75bn in allowable expenses against £58.99bn in rental income. This marks a significant shift from 2019-20, when expenses totalled £22.33bn against income of £46.69bn. The average landlord now faces £13,700 in expenses, compared to £20,500 in rental income.

Finance costs have emerged as the largest expense, accounting for 37% of total outgoings. Around 1.15 million landlords claimed residential finance costs averaging £11,148 each. Repairs and maintenance also represent a substantial portion of expenses, with 1.92 million landlords spending an average of £3,339 annually. These figures exclude capital improvements such as kitchen upgrades or energy efficiency measures.

Future Challenges for Landlords

Looking ahead, buy-to-let landlords face additional financial pressures. Privately rented homes in England must meet an EPC rating of C or higher by October 2030, unless exempt. Additionally, the reformed Decent Homes Standard is set to apply to the sector from 2035, potentially requiring further investment in property upgrades.

Mortgaged landlords are also grappling with the impact of Section 24, introduced in April 2020. This legislation prevents individual landlords from deducting residential finance costs when calculating taxable rental profits. Instead, they receive a basic-rate tax reduction worth 20% of these costs. Companies, however, remain unaffected by this restriction and can still deduct finance costs in full.

Phil Shelley, Chair of Hello Neighbour, noted: “A sector housing a fifth of the country cannot absorb costs rising at twice the rate of income indefinitely. Landlords are being asked to fund upgrades the country wants through increasingly squeezed margins.”

With costs continuing to rise faster than rental income, landlords may wish to carefully assess their financial position and consider strategies to manage expenses effectively in this challenging market.

item.title: July figures offer fresh warning for the housing market
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent HMRC data has revealed a slight dip in UK residential property transactions during July, raising fresh concerns about the housing market's resilience amidst ongoing economic uncertainty. Whilst seasonal adjustments show a 2% monthly decline, the broader picture remains more positive with year-to-date figures maintaining healthy growth compared to 2022 levels.

Mixed signals in transaction data

The provisional figures present two different perspectives on market activity. Seasonally adjusted completions fell to 96,710 in July – down from June's 98,390 and 1% below the same period last year. However, the non-adjusted data tells a more encouraging story, showing a 3% monthly increase to 106,620 transactions, representing a 5% annual uplift.

When examining the wider April-July period, the market appears stronger still. Some 389,490 non-seasonally adjusted residential transactions were recorded – a 15% increase compared to the same timeframe in 2022. Experts caution that these figures remain provisional and should be viewed as lagging indicators, typically reflecting sales agreed two to four months earlier.

Structural challenges persist

Industry voices have highlighted how the modest July dip underscores deeper systemic issues in the property market. Maria Harris of the Open Property Data Association noted: "The housing market remains vulnerable to uncertainty, but we must also address the structural problems making home moves unnecessarily difficult."

Key concerns include:

  • A fragmented and slow-moving transaction process
  • High rates of failed transactions due to inefficiencies
  • Lack of standardised property data sharing between parties

The government's proposed reforms to modernise homebuying could help address these challenges, though experts stress the importance of implementing robust data standards and secure information-sharing systems to make transactions more reliable.

Market caution continues

Mortgage professionals report that many potential movers remain hesitant, with Paul Adams of Pepper Money observing: "The brief improvement we saw in June hasn't developed into sustained growth." This aligns with broker feedback suggesting homeowners are:

  • Staying put to retain favourable mortgage rates secured in previous years
  • Adopting a wait-and-see approach amid economic uncertainty
  • Considering home improvements rather than moving in some cases

Whilst the housing market continues to demonstrate resilience compared to 2022's figures, these latest statistics serve as a reminder that underlying challenges persist. Both policymakers and industry participants may need to focus on modernising transaction processes to create a more efficient and reliable system for all involved.

item.title: Property industry reacts to latest Nationwide house price data
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK housing market showed little movement in August, with house prices rising by just 0.2%, according to the latest data from Nationwide. Annual house price growth remained steady at 1.6%, reflecting a market that continues to tread cautiously amidst ongoing economic uncertainty. Factors such as fluctuating interest rate expectations and rising energy costs have contributed to this subdued activity, though Nationwide suggests that the impact of energy prices on broader inflation may be limited.

Affordability Gradually Improves Amidst Challenges

Despite the sluggish market, Nationwide’s Chief Economist, Robert Gardner, noted that affordability is slowly improving. House price growth continues to lag behind earnings growth, which could benefit prospective buyers. However, higher mortgage rates have partially offset these gains, leaving many homeowners and potential buyers weighing their options. Gardner expressed optimism that market activity could regain momentum in the coming months, particularly if energy price pressures ease and confidence returns to the market.

Gardner also highlighted that private sector wage growth has shown signs of easing, potentially giving the Bank of England more flexibility in its monetary policy decisions. This could play a crucial role in determining whether further interest rate hikes are necessary to bring inflation back to target levels.

National Park Properties Command Premium Prices

In addition to its monthly house price analysis, Nationwide conducted research into the impact of location on property values, specifically focusing on homes within National Parks. The findings revealed that properties located in these areas attract a significant premium, averaging 24% higher than comparable homes elsewhere. In monetary terms, this equates to an additional £66,500 for a typical property.

Gardner explained that National Parks are highly sought-after due to their scenic landscapes and access to outdoor activities. Strict development controls, which limit new housing construction, also contribute to the higher prices. For homeowners considering a move to these areas, this premium reflects the unique appeal and limited availability of properties in such locations.

As the UK housing market navigates a period of uncertainty, these insights from Nationwide provide a clearer picture of current trends and potential opportunities for buyers and sellers alike.

item.title: New shadow housing secretary appointed after James Cleverly steps down
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Katie Lam MP has been named as the Conservative Party's new Shadow Housing, Communities and Local Government Secretary following Sir James Cleverly's resignation from the role. The change comes as Cleverly, MP for Braintree, prepares to seek his party's nomination for the 2028 London mayoral election. His departure from the shadow housing brief after just over a year in post creates an opportunity for fresh scrutiny of government housing policies under new leadership.

New Shadow Housing Secretary takes the reins

As the newly appointed shadow housing minister, Lam assumes responsibility for holding the government to account on key property market issues including housebuilding targets, planning system reforms and housing affordability. The Weald of Kent MP will also oversee local government and communities policy within her expanded brief. The Conservative Party emphasised Lam's dual focus on boosting housing supply while protecting local community interests in their announcement.

Lam steps into the role during a period of significant challenges for the housing sector, with ongoing debates about planning permission reforms and concerns about meeting annual housing construction targets. Industry commentators will be watching closely to see how the new shadow secretary approaches these longstanding issues that directly impact mortgage holders and prospective buyers.

Political context of the appointment

The shadow cabinet reshuffle occurs against the backdrop of Cleverly's mayoral ambitions, though he hasn't yet confirmed whether he'll resign as an MP. The Conservatives haven't selected their London mayoral candidate, leaving Cleverly's political future temporarily uncertain as he prepares his campaign. Meanwhile, Lam's promotion signals the opposition party's intention to strengthen its housing policy platform ahead of the next general election.

Housing professionals suggest Lam's background as a backbench MP with constituency experience dealing with local planning matters could prove valuable in scrutinising government housing strategies. Her appointment comes at a time when both major political parties are under pressure to address the UK's chronic housing shortage and make homeownership more accessible.

The property industry will be particularly interested to see whether Lam maintains Cleverly's policy direction or implements new approaches to housing supply and planning reforms. With affordability remaining a critical concern for borrowers and first-time buyers, political focus on these issues is likely to intensify in the coming months.

item.title: Frozen tax thresholds blamed for property market drag
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK property market is facing a slowdown, with frozen Stamp Duty thresholds and rising house prices creating significant barriers for buyers. Recent data from HMRC reveals a dip in residential property transactions, highlighting the challenges homeowners face in the current climate. Experts suggest that these factors, combined with broader economic pressures, are contributing to subdued activity across the housing market.

Rising Costs and Frozen Thresholds

House price growth, whilst slowing in some areas, continues to push more buyers into higher Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) brackets. The thresholds for SDLT have remained unchanged since 2014, meaning that as property values rise, more homeowners are liable for higher upfront costs when moving. This growing tax burden is becoming a notable obstacle for those looking to purchase a new home.

Mark Cunningham, a partner at Blick Rothenberg, an audit and advisory firm, explains: "Rising property values and frozen SDLT thresholds have resulted in a larger tax burden on most transactions, increasing the overall cost of moving." This is particularly challenging at a time when household budgets are already under pressure from higher borrowing costs and the wider cost of living crisis.

Impact on Market Activity

HMRC’s latest figures show that residential property transactions fell to 96,710 in July on a seasonally adjusted basis, down 2% from June and 1% compared to the same period last year. Whilst activity remains above the levels seen in parts of 2023 and early 2024, the market has yet to establish a sustained upward trend. Cunningham notes that SDLT is not the sole reason for subdued transaction levels, but it is a significant factor influencing buyer behaviour.

"As a transaction tax, SDLT increases the upfront cost of moving and is therefore likely to influence decisions, particularly when household finances are stretched," he adds. This raises questions about whether the government should consider adjusting SDLT thresholds to stimulate market activity.

The Need for Government Action

With housing remaining a key policy priority, there is a strong case for encouraging transactions alongside increasing supply. Cunningham argues: "The property market does not just need homes to be built. It also needs people to move. If transaction levels remain relatively flat despite a more settled economic backdrop, attention should turn to barriers preventing transactions from taking place."

As the government looks to address housing challenges, revising Stamp Duty thresholds could be one way to ease the financial burden on buyers and support a more dynamic property market.

For now, homeowners may wish to carefully consider the costs involved in moving, including SDLT, and explore options to mitigate these expenses. As the market continues to evolve, staying informed about potential changes to property taxes could prove invaluable for those planning their next move.

item.title: New initiative ‘is going to help transform homebuying’
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A new government-backed digital identity trust mark has launched this week, promising to streamline the often tedious process of identity verification during property transactions. The UK CertifID scheme allows approved Digital Verification Service (DVS) providers to display a trusted certification mark, potentially reducing the need for homebuyers to repeatedly prove their identity to different parties involved in their purchase.

How the trust mark could transform homebuying

Currently, property buyers typically need to verify their identity separately with estate agents, mortgage brokers, lenders and conveyancers – a repetitive process that can cause delays. The new scheme aims to create a reusable digital identity that moves with the transaction, allowing different professionals to rely on a single verified check.

Chris Williams of Novus Strategy commented: "After years of waiting, we're now on the cusp of only having to verify identity once. This could allow simultaneous progress on credit checks, underwriting and property searches – potentially reducing the current high rates of failed transactions."

Industry experts suggest the trust mark could particularly benefit:

  • First-time buyers navigating complex processes
  • Those remortgaging or moving home
  • Professionals handling high volumes of transactions

Security and adoption expectations

While participation remains optional for verification providers, market observers anticipate near-universal adoption across the property and lending sectors. The Office for Digital Identities and Attributes (OfDIA) oversees the scheme, which requires providers to meet stringent security standards.

"UK CertifID shows consumers which providers meet all necessary security requirements," Williams explained. "It also gives conveyancers confidence that earlier checks by brokers or agents were fully compliant and can be reused – this is Smart Data in action."

The system represents an example of Horizontal Digital Integration (HDI), where verified identity becomes a reusable component that travels securely with the transaction. As the scheme rolls out, homeowners may find:

  • Reduced paperwork and admin
  • Faster transaction timelines
  • Greater confidence in the security of their data

While the full impact remains to be seen, this initiative could mark a significant step towards modernising the UK's property transaction process – potentially benefiting all parties involved in home purchases and mortgage applications.

item.title: NRLA warns of risk of unqualified agents
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

With rental regulations becoming increasingly complex, the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) has raised concerns about unqualified letting agents operating without mandatory training standards. As more landlords turn to agents to navigate the evolving legal landscape, industry bodies are calling for swifter government action to implement minimum competency requirements.

The growing reliance on letting agents

Recent research suggests a significant proportion of private landlords now depend on letting agents to manage their properties and ensure compliance with housing legislation. The private rental sector has seen over 170 pieces of legislation introduced in the past decade alone, covering everything from tenant fees to safety standards.

Whilst professional agents can provide valuable expertise, the NRLA warns that the current lack of mandatory qualifications means landlords might inadvertently engage unqualified practitioners. This could potentially lead to:

  • Regulatory non-compliance and associated penalties
  • Poor tenant referencing and vetting processes
  • Inadequate property maintenance standards

Calls for industry-wide standards

The NRLA has joined other property organisations in urging the government to accelerate plans for a mandatory qualification framework. Currently, unlike estate agents who must register with a redress scheme, letting agents in England face no minimum training requirements - though Wales and Scotland have already introduced their own accreditation systems.

Industry proposals suggest that a national competency framework could include:

  • Standardised training on housing law and regulations
  • Continuous professional development requirements
  • Clear pathways for agent certification

Landlords using letting agents might wish to verify their current qualifications through recognised schemes such as Propertymark or the NRLA's own training programmes whilst awaiting potential regulatory changes.

As the government continues its review of the private rental sector, the debate around professional standards highlights the growing complexity of property management. With landlords facing increasing responsibilities, the call for properly qualified agents looks set to remain a key industry issue in the coming months.
